```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 5

```

leeward maps how sheltered terrain is from the wind. This vignette uses the
bundled example data, a 10 m DEM around Lake Vesuvius Recreation Area
(Wayne National Forest, Ohio) and five years of hourly winds from the
Huntington, WV ASOS station, so it runs offline.

Results identify **candidate areas to scout**, not safe campsites. Sheltered
hollows can flood, collect cold air, or sit under dead trees. Check current
rules with the managing agency.

```{r setup}
library(leeward)

dem <- terra::rast(
  system.file("extdata", "vesuvius_dem.tif", package = "leeward")
)
wind <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "hts_wind.csv", package = "leeward"))
```

## Wind climatology

Directions are degrees the wind blows **from**, 0 = north, clockwise. Filter
to the season you camp in before binning.

```{r}
summer <- wind[wind$month %in% 5:10, ]
freq <- wind_direction_freq(summer$drct, n_sectors = 16)
head(freq[order(-freq$frequency), ])
```

Speed classes are available if you want to see whether strong winds come
from different directions than light ones:

```{r}
by_speed <- wind_direction_freq(
  summer$drct,
  n_sectors = 8,
  speed = summer$sknt,
  speed_breaks = c(0, 5, 10, Inf)
)
xtabs(frequency ~ sector_center + speed_class, by_speed)
```

## Shelter from one direction

`exposure_along_direction()` computes the Winstral Sx index: the steepest
angle from each cell up (or down) to terrain within `max_dist` upwind.
Positive values are sheltered.

```{r}
sx_ssw <- exposure_along_direction(dem, direction = 202.5, max_dist = 300)
terra::plot(sx_ssw, main = "Sx, wind from SSW")
```

## Choosing max_dist

`max_dist` should roughly match the distance from where you would camp to
the nearest upwind ridgeline. If you leave it out, leeward picks a value from
the DEM's local relief and says so:

```{r}
suggest_max_dist(dem)
```

## Frequency-weighted shelter

`wind_exposure()` weights each sector's Sx by how often the wind blows from
it. Cells within `max_dist` of the DEM edge are `NA`, so clip your DEM with a
buffer of at least `max_dist` around the area you care about.

```{r}
sx <- wind_exposure(dem, freq, max_dist = 300)
terra::plot(sx, main = "Sx, May-October winds")
```

## Terrain and water layers

Suitability layers come in two kinds. **Scores** run from 0 to 1 and trade
off against each other. **Exclusions** are hard rules: `TRUE` means a cell is
out, however well it scores.

```{r}
flat <- flatness_score(dem, flat = 5, steep = 15)
facing <- aspect_score(dem, preferred_aspect = 135)
terra::plot(c(flat, facing))
```

`preferred_aspect` is the direction a slope *faces*, not a wind direction.

Water access and the setback come from the same distance raster:

```{r}
gpkg <- system.file("extdata", "vesuvius_water.gpkg", package = "leeward")
water <- list(
  terra::vect(gpkg, layer = "flowlines"),
  terra::vect(gpkg, layer = "waterbodies")
)
d <- water_distance(dem, water)
access <- water_score(d, setback = 61, reach = 800)
excluded <- water_exclusion(d, setback = 61)
terra::plot(access)
terra::plot(
  terra::ifel(excluded, 1, NA),
  col = "red", legend = FALSE, add = TRUE
)
```

Mapped streams miss many small hollows that carry water after storms. A
cell far from any mapped stream can still sit in a flash-flood channel.

## Channels from the DEM

`height_above_channel()` finds channels from the terrain itself: any cell
draining at least `min_area` (default 1 ha) is a channel, and every other
cell gets its height above the channel it drains to. Around Lake Vesuvius,
1 ha channels lie within 20 m of 98% of the mapped stream length, and
their total length is about three times the mapped length. Most of the
extra is in headwater hollows that the stream map leaves out.

```{r}
hand <- height_above_channel(dem, min_area = 1e4)
low <- channel_exclusion(hand, min_height = 3)
terra::plot(hand, main = "Height above channel (m)")
terra::plot(
  terra::ifel(low | excluded, 1, NA),
  col = "red", legend = FALSE, add = TRUE
)
```

The red area combines both exclusions. It is a minimum hazard area: a 10 m
DEM cannot show narrow gullies or culverts. Cells that drain off the DEM
without reaching a channel are `NA`, which means unknown, not safe.

## Putting it together

`camp_suitability()` takes a weighted mean of the scores and applies every
exclusion as a hard rule. A cell that is `NA` in any exclusion is treated as
excluded, because `NA` means unknown, not safe. There are no default weights:
these are examples, so set your own for the trip.

```{r}
shelter <- shelter_score(sx, exposed = 0, sheltered = 10)
suit <- camp_suitability(
  scores = list(
    shelter = shelter, flat = flat, aspect = facing, water = access
  ),
  weights = c(shelter = 2, flat = 3, aspect = 1, water = 1),
  exclusions = list(excluded, low)
)
terra::plot(suit$suitability, main = "Suitability (example weights)")
```

`candidate_areas()` turns the best cells into ranked polygons:

```{r}
sites <- candidate_areas(suit, min_score = 0.7, min_area = 400)
head(as.data.frame(sites))
terra::plot(suit$suitability, main = "Candidate areas, rank 1-10")
terra::plot(sites[sites$rank <= 10], add = TRUE, border = "red", lwd = 2)
```

These are **candidate areas to scout**, not campsites. Edge bands from
`max_dist`, the exclusions, and the 10 m grid all limit what the model can
see. Visit each area, check the trees overhead and the ground underfoot,
and confirm the rules with the managing agency.

## TOPEX

When no nearby wind record exists, `topex()` sums skyline angles over eight
directions with equal weight. The 500 m default distance follows Quine and
White (1998).

```{r}
tx <- topex(dem)
terra::plot(tx, main = "TOPEX, 500 m")
```
